source_text: Sed quid dicam de ueritate atque sapientia, quae omnes potentias animae superat. cum ipsius animae natura, quae mutabilis inuenitur, nullo modo locorum spatia quadam mole sua occupet.? quicquid enim qualibet crassitudine est, non potest nisi minui per partes habendo aliud hic et aliud alibi. minor est enim digitus quam tota manus et minor est digitus unus quam duo et alibi est iste digitus. alibi ille, alibi cetera manus. quod non solum in molibus corporum articulatis uidemus, sed etiam terrae pars ista non est ibi, ubi illa, quia suum locum quaeque obtinet; et pars umoris minor minore et maior maiore loco est; et alia pars est circa fundum, alia circa oras poculi. similiter aeris partes suos quaeque inplent locos. nec fieri potest, ut aer, quo inpletur haec domus, simul secum in eadem domo habere possit etiam illum aerem, quem uicini habent. lucisque ipsius alia pars infunditur per hanc fenestram, alia per illam, et maior per maiorem, per minorem autem minor. nec omnino potest esse aliquod corpus siue caeleste siue terrestre siue aerium siue umidum, quod non minus sit in parte quam in toto: neque ullo modo possit in loco huius partis simul habere aliam partem, sed aliud hic et aliud alibi habens per quaelibet spatia locorum distanti et diuidua, uel potius, ut ita dicam, sectili mole distenditur. animae uero natura, etiamsi non illa eius potentia consideretur, qua intellegit ueritatem, sed illa inferior, qua continet corpus et sentit in corpore, nullo modo inuenitur locorum spatiis aliqua mole distendi. nam singulis sui corporis particulis tota praesto est, cum tota sentit in singulis; nec minor pars eius in digito est et maior in brachio, sicut ipse digitus brachio minor est, sed ubique tanta est, quia ubique tota est. cum enim tangitur digitus. non per totum corpus sentit, et tamen tota sentit. totam enim tactus ille non latet; quod non fieret. nisi tota praesto esset. nec sic tota praesto est, cum tangitur digitus et sentit in digito. ut ceterum deserat corpus et sese ad unum illum locum. in quo sentit, adglomeret. sed cum tota sentit in digito manus, si alius locus tangatur in pede. nec ibi desinit tota sentire. atque ita in singulis distantibus locis tota simul adest. non unum deserens. ut in altero tota sit, neque ita utrumque tenens. ut aliam partem hic habeat et alibi aliam. sed sufficiens exhibere se singulis locis simul totam, quoniam tota sentit in singulis satis ostendit se locorum spatiis non teneri.
thought_title: The soul is not extended through space
orientation: Augustine is arguing against Mani's picture of God as a bodily mass, and now turns to the soul to show that even a mutable nature is not spread out through places.
pass_a_gloss: But what [shall] I say about truth and wisdom, which surpass all powers of [the] soul. when the nature of [the] soul itself, which is found changeable, in no way occupies [the] spaces of places by some mass of its own.? for whatever is of any thickness, cannot except be diminished through parts by having one [thing] here and another elsewhere. for smaller is [the] finger than [the] whole hand and smaller is one finger than two and elsewhere is this finger. elsewhere that [one], elsewhere [the] rest of [the] hand. which not only in [the] articulated masses of bodies we see, but also this part of [the] earth is not there, where that [part], because each [part] holds its own place; and [the] part of moisture [is] in [a] smaller [place] [when] smaller and in [a] larger [place] [when] larger; and one part is around [the] bottom, another around [the] edges of [the] cup. similarly [the] parts of air each fill their own places. nor can it happen, that [the] air, by which this house is filled, at [the] same time with itself in [the] same house can have also that air, which [the] neighbors have. and of light itself one part is poured in through this window, another through that [one], and [a] greater [part] through [a] greater [window], but through [a] smaller [window] [a] smaller [part]. nor at all can there be any body whether heavenly or earthly or airy or moist, which [is] not less in [its] part than in [the] whole: nor in any way could it in [the] place of this part at [the] same time have another part, but having one [thing] here and another elsewhere through any spaces of places [it] is stretched out [as] distant and divided, or rather, so that I may say [it] thus, [as] [a] cuttable mass. but [the] nature of [the] soul, even if not that power of it is considered, by which it understands [the] truth, but that lower [power], by which it holds [the] body and senses in [the] body, in no way is found to be stretched out by any mass [in] [the] spaces of places. for to [the] single small parts of its own body [the] whole is present, when [the] whole senses in [the] single [parts]; nor [is] [a] smaller part of it in [the] finger and [a] greater [part] in [the] arm, just as [the] finger itself is smaller than [the] arm, but everywhere [it] is [as] great, because everywhere [it] is whole. for when [the] finger is touched. [it] does not sense through [the] whole body, and yet [the] whole senses. for that touch does not escape [the] whole; which would not happen. unless [the] whole were present. nor [is] [the] whole thus present, when [the] finger is touched and [it] senses in [the] finger. that [it] should desert [the] rest of [the] body and gather itself to that one place. in which [it] senses. but when [the] whole senses in [the] finger of [the] hand, if another place is touched in [the] foot. nor there does [the] whole cease to sense. and so in [the] single distant places [the] whole at [the] same time is present. not deserting one [place]. that [it] may be whole in [the] other, nor thus holding both. that [it] may have one part here and another elsewhere. but [being] sufficient to present itself to [the] single places at [the] same time whole, since [the] whole senses in [the] single [places] [it] sufficiently shows itself not to be held by [the] spaces of places.

choices.english: with some bulk of its own
choices.why: Keeps the ablative of means and the dismissive 'quadam' ('some') to show Augustine's point that the soul has no bulk at all.
rejected: by any mass of its own

choices.why: Renders the rare 'sectilis' literally as 'cuttable' to preserve the image of a body that can be divided, which Augustine contrasts with the soul.
Keeps the repeated 'tota' ('wholly') and 'praesto' ('present') as a fixed phrase, since Augustine uses it as a technical description of the soul's presence.
rejected: the whole of it is available

choices.why: The verb suggests a piling or crowding together into one place; 'gathers itself' keeps the reflexive force and the spatial image.

choices.english: it is not held by the spaces of places
choices.why: Keeps the passive infinitive 'teneri' ('to be held') and the genitive 'locorum spatiis' literally, preserving Augustine's claim that the soul is not constrained by spatial extension.
rejected: it is not confined to spatial intervals
it is not bound by local spaces

pass_b_english: But what shall I say of truth and wisdom, which surpass every power of the soul, when the nature of the soul itself, which is found to be mutable, in no way occupies the spaces of places with some bulk of its own? For whatever has any thickness cannot help but be diminished through its parts, having one thing here and another elsewhere. A finger is smaller than the whole hand, and one finger is smaller than two, and this finger is in one place, that finger in another, and the rest of the hand elsewhere. We see this not only in the jointed masses of bodies, but also in the earth: this part of it is not where that part is, because each part occupies its own place. A smaller part of moisture occupies a smaller place, a larger part a larger place; one part is near the bottom, another near the rim of the cup. Likewise the parts of air each fill their own places. Nor can it happen that the air which fills this house can at the same time have within the same house also that air which the neighbors have. Of light itself, one part pours in through this window, another through that one, and more through a larger window, less through a smaller one. Nor can there be any body at all—whether heavenly or earthly, airy or moist—that is not less in its part than in its whole, nor can it in any way have another part at the same time in the place of this part. Rather, having one thing here and another elsewhere, it is stretched out through whatever spaces of places with a distant and divided, or rather, so to speak, cuttable bulk.

But the nature of the soul—even if we consider not that power of it by which it understands truth, but that lower power by which it holds the body together and senses in the body—is in no way found to be stretched out through the spaces of places by any bulk. For it is wholly present to each single particle of its body, since it senses wholly in each one. Its part in the finger is not smaller and its part in the arm larger, as the finger itself is smaller than the arm; rather, it is as great everywhere because it is wholly everywhere. For when the finger is touched, it does not sense through the whole body, and yet it senses wholly. That touch does not escape the whole of it, which would not happen unless it were wholly present. Nor is it wholly present in such a way that, when the finger is touched and it senses in the finger, it abandons the rest of the body and gathers itself to that one place where it senses. But when it senses wholly in the finger of the hand, if another place is touched on the foot, it does not cease to sense wholly there either. And so in single distant places it is wholly present at the same time—not abandoning one place so that it may be wholly in another, nor holding both in such a way that it has one part here and another elsewhere, but able to present itself wholly to single places at the same time. Since it senses wholly in each one, it shows clearly enough that it is not held by the spaces of places.

last_rejected.quote: For whatever has any thickness cannot help but be diminished through its parts
last_rejected.source_quote: quicquid enim qualibet crassitudine est, non potest nisi minui per partes habendo aliud hic et aliud alibi
last_rejected.why: "cannot help but be diminished" misreads minui: things with thickness are diminished by being in parts, not that they "cannot help but be diminished" as a necessity.
last_rejected.fix: For whatever has any thickness, by having parts, is necessarily lessened, having one thing here and another elsewhere.
last_rejected.ruling: non potest nisi minui = 'cannot but be diminished'; 'cannot help but be diminished' correctly captures the Latin necessity.

last_rejected.quote: it is stretched out through whatever spaces of places with a distant and divided, or rather, so to speak, cuttable bulk
last_rejected.source_quote: per quaelibet spatia locorum distanti et diuidua, uel potius, ut ita dicam, sectili mole distenditur
last_rejected.why: "distant and divided" mistranslates distanti et diuidua (ablative agreeing with mole): the bulk itself is distended, distant, divided, and cuttable—not "through spaces with a distant...bulk."
last_rejected.fix: it is stretched through whatever spaces of places by a bulk that is distant and divided, or rather, so to speak, cuttable.
last_rejected.ruling: distanti et diuidua...mole: English 'with a distant and divided...bulk' correctly attaches modifiers to bulk; 'through spaces' renders per spatia.

last_rejected.quote: Its part in the finger is not smaller and its part in the arm larger
last_rejected.source_quote: nec minor pars eius in digito est et maior in brachio
last_rejected.why: English adds "Its part" twice, making it sound like the soul has parts; but Augustine denies this. The Latin says "nor is a smaller part of it in the finger and a larger in the arm"—a hypothetical the soul does not satisfy.
last_rejected.fix: nor is a smaller part of it in the finger and a larger in the arm
last_rejected.ruling: 'Its part' translates pars eius; Latin states the hypothetical. English 'is not smaller' negates it, preserving Augustine's denial of soul-parts.

last_rejected.quote: it does not sense through the whole body, and yet it senses wholly
last_rejected.source_quote: non per totum corpus sentit, et tamen tota sentit
last_rejected.why: "it does not sense through the whole body" misrepresents non per totum corpus sentit: the soul doesn't sense in the whole body (when finger is touched), not that it doesn't sense "through" the body.
last_rejected.fix: it does not sense in the whole body, and yet it senses wholly
last_rejected.ruling: non per totum corpus sentit = 'does not sense through the whole body'; 'through' correctly renders per, contrasting localized touch with whole-soul presence.
